compare_blocks.body:
The table assumes aligned conditions: the same offer, the same disclosed information, the same household situation and the same reply deadline. If one person has worked in the field for ten years and the other is switching in, experience will swamp both columns; if one is the household's main earner, the room for risk differs too.

Each row is written as a shared question against the evidence likely to be consulted first, and each row states whether it illustrates S/N or T/F. Both types can use both approaches; the table only describes what tends to be taken first under the same conditions. Because both share J, "forming an arrangement outward" is not a difference here and gets no column.

| Shared question about the same offer | INFJ: evidence likely to be consulted first | ISTJ: evidence likely to be consulted first | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Where does this job put me in three or four years | What patterns in the same role information suggest about where the work could lead | Where people in similar roles went in recent years, and how often this business line has been reorganised | Information gathering: S/N |

compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In a fictional meeting, both colleagues take time to consider the same proposal before commenting. Someone could behave that way because of the role they have, how familiar they are with the topic, or what the meeting expects. A quiet meeting tells you little about either person's type.

I describes a preference for directing attention and energy inward. J describes a preference for structure and clear arrangements when dealing with the outer world. Neither letter tells you how quickly someone will speak or make a decision.

S/N concerns the information a person tends to emphasize: observable facts and relevant experience, or patterns and possibilities. T/F concerns how a person weighs a decision: by consistent criteria, or by considering people and values. Everyone can draw on both sides of each pair.

### INFJ and ISTJ: one plan, two kinds of evidence

In a fictional meeting, two colleagues review the same departmental reorganization proposal.

One reading looks for the direction implied by the proposal: which responsibilities might grow and which problems the change could solve. Another checks which roles are affected, how long the handover lasts, and what happened during a comparable reorganization. Either colleague can ask both sets of questions.

Both kinds of evidence can inform the decision. An emerging pattern can suggest where to look next, while the documented terms can show whether that possibility is feasible.

In a fictional example at home, two people consider replacing a parent's washing machine. One considers what a new machine might change about the care routine. Another checks the available space and installation requirements. Either person can consider both.

This is useful in a review meeting. Hearing "this direction will not hold" and "these three items are not verified yet", there is no need to decide who is more reliable: the first names a gap in possibility, the second a gap in fact. Put side by side, the plan is complete.

### INFJ and ISTJ: why I and J are shared while no function name is

In the four-function notation used here, INFJ is Ni–Fe–Ti–Se and ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne. Line the two up and each seat reads Ni against Si, Fe against Te, Ti against Fi, Se against Ne: no name repeats.

In this framework, both IJ types lead with an introverted perceiving process and use an extraverted judging process as their auxiliary. S/N changes which perceiving processes appear and T/F changes which judging processes appear. Under the notation used here, the orientation matches at each corresponding position even though the function names differ.

So a comparison has to say which method it uses. By position, the attitudes match and the processes differ. By process — Ni against Ne, Fe against Fi — the attitudes reverse and the positions move as well. Mixing the two produces the claim that all four pairs are reversed, which matches neither names nor positions.

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted is not uniform across sources: this page marks the attitude for INFJ's Ti and ISTJ's Fi, and other tables give only the function name. When a different version turns up, check first whether it names its source. The disagreement does not change the first two positions, and it does not explain how quickly someone acts, what they are good at, or whom they get along with. Base descriptions sit on the [INFJ profile](/en/personality/infj) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).

compare_blocks.body:
Boundary of use: both scenes below show one matter being read with different emphasis. They are not a way of deciding who can do which job or who is better with children. Real trade-offs depend on the facts, experience and resources the people actually have, and type does not enter the evaluation.

People can disagree about whether the direction is convincing or whether there is enough detail to act. Those questions can be useful together, whichever person raises them.

### INFJ and ISTJ: whether to take this offer

(Fictional scene) An offer is on the table: a twenty per cent raise, a move to another city, a shift from familiar work into a new direction, and one week to answer.

In this fictional scene, one approach runs the shape of the path through the mind: whether what the company does matches what I believe in, whether I would regret this in three years, whether I could tolerate the atmosphere in that team. The other lays the terms out flat: pre-tax pay, probation length, benefits and required payroll contributions, commuting time, grade and raise rules, and then one further question — "has anyone held this role in the past two years, and where did they go". Either type can combine both kinds of evidence; which step gets taken depends on division of labour, authority and the information already in hand.

Each approach has a conditional blind spot. Someone following the direction alone may never check the precise wording of probation and review, and discover in the first appraisal that the definitions are not what they assumed. Someone checking clause by clause may account for every item and never ask whether they want to stay in the job. Both omissions happen to both types; it depends on what information is available and whether the household can absorb a bad outcome.

One low-effort check is to price the reversal: write down how long it would take to undo a wrong choice and what that would cost. If the answer is "six months and a moving bill", the discussion naturally moves to specific terms. If it is "three years and no route back into the old industry", it has to return to direction. Either type can do this, and who proposes it first has nothing to do with type.

Worth noting: both may count money first for the family's sake, and either may suddenly change their mind at some stage. Changing one's mind is not itself evidence of type; what matters is which kind of reason gets cited when the change happens.

### INFJ and ISTJ: choosing an after-school class

(Fictional scene) A seven-year-old wants to learn drawing and also wants to learn robotics. There are only two half-days at the weekend, and a year of either is a real expense.

In this fictional scene, one approach watches the state the child is in while saying it: which idea is his own and which comes from a classmate, and where the course might lead — a childhood scheduled full, or a hobby he can inhabit on his own. The other lays out the conditions: how many minutes to get there, the price per lesson, the teacher's qualifications, whether three years is realistic, how missed lessons are made up — then takes the child to a trial lesson of each and watches whether he can sit through it. Either type can combine both kinds of evidence; which step gets taken depends on division of labour, authority and the information already in hand.

Both sides are actually collecting the same material: the child's willingness, his response in the trial, the family's time and budget, how far the course can go. The difference is which part gets picked up first and which gets trusted first. Reading only the child's eyes may sign him up for something lively that stops after two years; counting only hours and price may produce a child who dawdles at the door every week while the money is spent and nobody goes. Neither risk belongs to one type.

The review step is to ask rather than conclude on the child's behalf: after the trial, do not enrol immediately — let the child say whether he wants to come back, then ask why. A child who cannot explain is normal; book another trial or ask the teacher what they observed. Put the budget and the transport arrangement on the table at the same time, so that "wanting to" and "being able to" are visible together.

What genuinely needs agreeing in advance is when it can stop. Settling on a number of lessons before a joint review gives both an observation window and a clear exit point; the number follows the course rhythm and the household situation, and does not need to copy anyone else's figure.

compare_blocks.body:
The first misread takes I for unsociable. An INFJ can talk until late in a one-to-one; an ISTJ tells jokes among colleagues they know. Introversion describes where attention and energy tend to go, not social performance, and not a dislike of people.

The second treats T and F as hard and soft. An ISTJ can hold a hard line about someone they care about; an INFJ can analyse cause and effect without mercy. Judging type by whether today's remarks felt warm reads the setting and the mood, not a preference. Talking about meaning and keeping to the rules are both learnable expressions, on a different layer from the four letters.

The third stops at "both have strong opinions" and calls it a shared trait. Having opinions is the surface; the source is the point. One more often works back from direction to conditions, the other forward from precedent. Without that distinction, any advice about getting along together misses.

The fourth uses who speaks or moves first as evidence. In the same household task, the person who moves first is often simply the one who knows the situation better; duty, experience and how many people are present all rewrite the order.

items.question: Can an ISTJ talk about meaning, and an INFJ follow the rules?

items.answer:
One more often asks whether this path leads where they want to go; the other more often asks whether the job can be done steadily and by what rules one advances.

items.question: In a career decision, what does each look at?

items.answer:
Not by type, but by the relative's wishes, each person's caring experience, available time and what the care actually requires — and by naming who talks, who records and who double-checks.

For example, one person talks with the relative and draws out the worries, while the other builds the rota, records medication times, and keeps the test results and reimbursement paperwork in order. That is a division of labour, not a type assignment, and the reverse arrangement is common. Medication, follow-up plans and whether to go to hospital are for the doctor to decide; in an emergency, seek help first, call the local emergency number and follow the dispatcher's or attending clinician's instructions, while the household's job is to bring the observed facts and records along.

body: In a fictional meeting, both colleagues take time to consider the same proposal before commenting. Someone could behave that way because of the role they have, how familiar they are with the topic, or what the meeting expects. A quiet meeting tells you little about either person's type.

I describes a preference for directing attention and energy inward. J describes a preference for structure and clear arrangements when dealing with the outer world. Neither letter tells you how quickly someone will speak or make a decision.

S/N concerns the information a person tends to emphasize: observable facts and relevant experience, or patterns and possibilities. T/F concerns how a person weighs a decision: by consistent criteria, or by considering people and values. Everyone can draw on both sides of each pair.
### INFJ and ISTJ: one plan, two kinds of evidence
In a fictional meeting, two colleagues review the same departmental reorganization proposal.

One reading looks for the direction implied by the proposal: which responsibilities might grow and which problems the change could solve. Another checks which roles are affected, how long the handover lasts, and what happened during a comparable reorganization. Either colleague can ask both sets of questions.
Both kinds of evidence can inform the decision. An emerging pattern can suggest where to look next, while the documented terms can show whether that possibility is feasible.

In a fictional example at home, two people consider replacing a parent's washing machine. One considers what a new machine might change about the care routine. Another checks the available space and installation requirements. Either person can consider both.

This is useful in a review meeting. Hearing "this direction will not hold" and "these three items are not verified yet", there is no need to decide who is more reliable: the first names a gap in possibility, the second a gap in fact. Put side by side, the plan is complete.
### INFJ and ISTJ: why I and J are shared while no function name is
In the four-function notation used here, INFJ is Ni–Fe–Ti–Se and ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne. Line the two up and each seat reads Ni against Si, Fe against Te, Ti against Fi, Se against Ne: no name repeats.

In this framework, both IJ types lead with an introverted perceiving process and use an extraverted judging process as their auxiliary. S/N changes which perceiving processes appear and T/F changes which judging processes appear. Under the notation used here, the orientation matches at each corresponding position even though the function names differ.

So a comparison has to say which method it uses. By position, the attitudes match and the processes differ. By process — Ni against Ne, Fe against Fi — the attitudes reverse and the positions move as well. Mixing the two produces the claim that all four pairs are reversed, which matches neither names nor positions.

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted is not uniform across sources: this page marks the attitude for INFJ's Ti and ISTJ's Fi, and other tables give only the function name. When a different version turns up, check first whether it names its source. The disagreement does not change the first two positions, and it does not explain how quickly someone acts, what they are good at, or whom they get along with. Base descriptions sit on the [INFJ profile](/en/personality/infj) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).

body: The table assumes aligned conditions: the same offer, the same disclosed information, the same household situation and the same reply deadline. If one person has worked in the field for ten years and the other is switching in, experience will swamp both columns; if one is the household's main earner, the room for risk differs too.

Each row is written as a shared question against the evidence likely to be consulted first, and each row states whether it illustrates S/N or T/F. Both types can use both approaches; the table only describes what tends to be taken first under the same conditions. Because both share J, "forming an arrangement outward" is not a difference here and gets no column.

| Shared question about the same offer | INFJ: evidence likely to be consulted first | ISTJ: evidence likely to be consulted first | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Where does this job put me in three or four years | What patterns in the same role information suggest about where the work could lead | Where people in similar roles went in recent years, and how often this business line has been reorganised | Information gathering: S/N |
| Both choose which terms to negotiate from the same confirmed offer | Weigh how the review and probation terms would affect the people doing the work | Apply the same criteria for pay, review and probation to each option | Decision criteria: T/F |
| What the household has to absorb | How far a partner's and children's lives have to move, how they feel about it, whether they can accept it | Moving costs, commuting time, the practical arrangements for changing schools and pick-ups | Both types check family circumstances and actual outlay |
| How to prioritize requests in the negotiation | Weigh how each request would affect the people who would have to carry out the agreement | Rank the same requests by criteria that can be applied consistently, such as cost and feasibility | Decision criteria: T/F |
| A side opportunity appears outside the job description | Whether this branch could grow into the direction I want, and whether it is worth betting on | Whether anyone has gone that way, at what rate of success and at what cost | Information gathering: S/N |

body: Boundary of use: both scenes below show one matter being read with different emphasis. They are not a way of deciding who can do which job or who is better with children. Real trade-offs depend on the facts, experience and resources the people actually have, and type does not enter the evaluation.
People can disagree about whether the direction is convincing or whether there is enough detail to act. Those questions can be useful together, whichever person raises them.
### INFJ and ISTJ: whether to take this offer
(Fictional scene) An offer is on the table: a twenty per cent raise, a move to another city, a shift from familiar work into a new direction, and one week to answer.

In this fictional scene, one approach runs the shape of the path through the mind: whether what the company does matches what I believe in, whether I would regret this in three years, whether I could tolerate the atmosphere in that team. The other lays the terms out flat: pre-tax pay, probation length, benefits and required payroll contributions, commuting time, grade and raise rules, and then one further question — "has anyone held this role in the past two years, and where did they go". Either type can combine both kinds of evidence; which step gets taken depends on division of labour, authority and the information already in hand.

Each approach has a conditional blind spot. Someone following the direction alone may never check the precise wording of probation and review, and discover in the first appraisal that the definitions are not what they assumed. Someone checking clause by clause may account for every item and never ask whether they want to stay in the job. Both omissions happen to both types; it depends on what information is available and whether the household can absorb a bad outcome.

One low-effort check is to price the reversal: write down how long it would take to undo a wrong choice and what that would cost. If the answer is "six months and a moving bill", the discussion naturally moves to specific terms. If it is "three years and no route back into the old industry", it has to return to direction. Either type can do this, and who proposes it first has nothing to do with type.

Worth noting: both may count money first for the family's sake, and either may suddenly change their mind at some stage. Changing one's mind is not itself evidence of type; what matters is which kind of reason gets cited when the change happens.
### INFJ and ISTJ: choosing an after-school class
(Fictional scene) A seven-year-old wants to learn drawing and also wants to learn robotics. There are only two half-days at the weekend, and a year of either is a real expense.

In this fictional scene, one approach watches the state the child is in while saying it: which idea is his own and which comes from a classmate, and where the course might lead — a childhood scheduled full, or a hobby he can inhabit on his own. The other lays out the conditions: how many minutes to get there, the price per lesson, the teacher's qualifications, whether three years is realistic, how missed lessons are made up — then takes the child to a trial lesson of each and watches whether he can sit through it. Either type can combine both kinds of evidence; which step gets taken depends on division of labour, authority and the information already in hand.

Both sides are actually collecting the same material: the child's willingness, his response in the trial, the family's time and budget, how far the course can go. The difference is which part gets picked up first and which gets trusted first. Reading only the child's eyes may sign him up for something lively that stops after two years; counting only hours and price may produce a child who dawdles at the door every week while the money is spent and nobody goes. Neither risk belongs to one type.

The review step is to ask rather than conclude on the child's behalf: after the trial, do not enrol immediately — let the child say whether he wants to come back, then ask why. A child who cannot explain is normal; book another trial or ask the teacher what they observed. Put the budget and the transport arrangement on the table at the same time, so that "wanting to" and "being able to" are visible together.

What genuinely needs agreeing in advance is when it can stop. Settling on a number of lessons before a joint review gives both an observation window and a clear exit point; the number follows the course rhythm and the household situation, and does not need to copy anyone else's figure.

comparison_public_projection_v1.summary:
INFJ and ISTJ share Introversion (I) and Judging (J). They differ in how they prefer to take in information (Sensing or Intuition) and which criteria they tend to weigh in decisions (Thinking or Feeling).

- I (Introversion): attention and energy turn more often toward the inner world — one's own ideas, impressions and sorting. It describes direction, not social skill, and people of both types may talk a great deal among friends.
- J (Judging): in dealings with the outer world, structure, arrangement and definiteness are preferred. It does not mean stubbornness, and it does not mean that everything is planned before anyone moves.
- S/N: the ISTJ side more often takes observable facts and prior experience first; the INFJ side more often takes connections between pieces of information, patterns and possibility first.
- T/F: the ISTJ side more often judges by impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently; the INFJ side more often puts people and values into the judgement.

In the type-dynamics notation used here, INFJ is Ni–Fe–Ti–Se and ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne. Both lead with an inward-facing process for taking in information, Ni for INFJ and Si for ISTJ, and both use an outward-facing decision process as their auxiliary, Fe and Te respectively. Sources differ on how to label the third process.

These preferences describe emphasis inside the model. They do not predict who speaks first, and they do not predict who is suited to which work. Facing the same decision, either type may check the terms first, and either may ask whether the thing is worth doing at all; order depends more on role, duty, experience and deadline.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
In a fictional meeting, both colleagues take time to consider the same proposal before commenting. Someone could behave that way because of the role they have, how familiar they are with the topic, or what the meeting expects. A quiet meeting tells you little about either person's type.

I describes a preference for directing attention and energy inward. J describes a preference for structure and clear arrangements when dealing with the outer world. Neither letter tells you how quickly someone will speak or make a decision.

S/N concerns the information a person tends to emphasize: observable facts and relevant experience, or patterns and possibilities. T/F concerns how a person weighs a decision: by consistent criteria, or by considering people and values. Everyone can draw on both sides of each pair.

### INFJ and ISTJ: one plan, two kinds of evidence

In a fictional meeting, two colleagues review the same departmental reorganization proposal.

One reading looks for the direction implied by the proposal: which responsibilities might grow and which problems the change could solve. Another checks which roles are affected, how long the handover lasts, and what happened during a comparable reorganization. Either colleague can ask both sets of questions.

Both kinds of evidence can inform the decision. An emerging pattern can suggest where to look next, while the documented terms can show whether that possibility is feasible.

In a fictional example at home, two people consider replacing a parent's washing machine. One considers what a new machine might change about the care routine. Another checks the available space and installation requirements. Either person can consider both.

This is useful in a review meeting. Hearing "this direction will not hold" and "these three items are not verified yet", there is no need to decide who is more reliable: the first names a gap in possibility, the second a gap in fact. Put side by side, the plan is complete.

### INFJ and ISTJ: why I and J are shared while no function name is

In the four-function notation used here, INFJ is Ni–Fe–Ti–Se and ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne. Line the two up and each seat reads Ni against Si, Fe against Te, Ti against Fi, Se against Ne: no name repeats.

In this framework, both IJ types lead with an introverted perceiving process and use an extraverted judging process as their auxiliary. S/N changes which perceiving processes appear and T/F changes which judging processes appear. Under the notation used here, the orientation matches at each corresponding position even though the function names differ.

So a comparison has to say which method it uses. By position, the attitudes match and the processes differ. By process — Ni against Ne, Fe against Fi — the attitudes reverse and the positions move as well. Mixing the two produces the claim that all four pairs are reversed, which matches neither names nor positions.

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted is not uniform across sources: this page marks the attitude for INFJ's Ti and ISTJ's Fi, and other tables give only the function name. When a different version turns up, check first whether it names its source. The disagreement does not change the first two positions, and it does not explain how quickly someone acts, what they are good at, or whom they get along with. Base descriptions sit on the [INFJ profile](/en/personality/infj) and the [ISTJ profile](/en/personality/istj).
sections.title: INFJ and ISTJ: shared ground and the core difference

sections.body_md:
The table assumes aligned conditions: the same offer, the same disclosed information, the same household situation and the same reply deadline. If one person has worked in the field for ten years and the other is switching in, experience will swamp both columns; if one is the household's main earner, the room for risk differs too.

Each row is written as a shared question against the evidence likely to be consulted first, and each row states whether it illustrates S/N or T/F. Both types can use both approaches; the table only describes what tends to be taken first under the same conditions. Because both share J, "forming an arrangement outward" is not a difference here and gets no column.

| Shared question about the same offer | INFJ: evidence likely to be consulted first | ISTJ: evidence likely to be consulted first | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Where does this job put me in three or four years | What patterns in the same role information suggest about where the work could lead | Where people in similar roles went in recent years, and how often this business line has been reorganised | Information gathering: S/N |
| Both choose which terms to negotiate from the same confirmed offer | Weigh how the review and probation terms would affect the people doing the work | Apply the same criteria for pay, review and probation to each option | Decision criteria: T/F |
| What the household has to absorb | How far a partner's and children's lives have to move, how they feel about it, whether they can accept it | Moving costs, commuting time, the practical arrangements for changing schools and pick-ups | Both types check family circumstances and actual outlay |
| How to prioritize requests in the negotiation | Weigh how each request would affect the people who would have to carry out the agreement | Rank the same requests by criteria that can be applied consistently, such as cost and feasibility | Decision criteria: T/F |
| A side opportunity appears outside the job description | Whether this branch could grow into the direction I want, and whether it is worth betting on | Whether anyone has gone that way, at what rate of success and at what cost | Information gathering: S/N |
| Looking back on this choice a year later | Weigh how the same choice affected the people who had to live with it | Apply the same review criteria to the documented outcomes | Decision criteria: T/F |

None of these rows is a scale of ability. Someone who has recruited for years will more likely compare a contract clause by clause whatever their type; someone changing jobs for the first time may say yes on the strength of "this work sounds interesting". Experience changes the behaviour without dictating its direction. The same person will also switch approaches depending on savings, who at home needs care, and how many days remain before a reply is due, so these rows cannot be used to classify anyone.
sections.title: INFJ and ISTJ in one minute

sections.body_md:
Boundary of use: both scenes below show one matter being read with different emphasis. They are not a way of deciding who can do which job or who is better with children. Real trade-offs depend on the facts, experience and resources the people actually have, and type does not enter the evaluation.

People can disagree about whether the direction is convincing or whether there is enough detail to act. Those questions can be useful together, whichever person raises them.

### INFJ and ISTJ: whether to take this offer

(Fictional scene) An offer is on the table: a twenty per cent raise, a move to another city, a shift from familiar work into a new direction, and one week to answer.

In this fictional scene, one approach runs the shape of the path through the mind: whether what the company does matches what I believe in, whether I would regret this in three years, whether I could tolerate the atmosphere in that team. The other lays the terms out flat: pre-tax pay, probation length, benefits and required payroll contributions, commuting time, grade and raise rules, and then one further question — "has anyone held this role in the past two years, and where did they go". Either type can combine both kinds of evidence; which step gets taken depends on division of labour, authority and the information already in hand.

Each approach has a conditional blind spot. Someone following the direction alone may never check the precise wording of probation and review, and discover in the first appraisal that the definitions are not what they assumed. Someone checking clause by clause may account for every item and never ask whether they want to stay in the job. Both omissions happen to both types; it depends on what information is available and whether the household can absorb a bad outcome.

One low-effort check is to price the reversal: write down how long it would take to undo a wrong choice and what that would cost. If the answer is "six months and a moving bill", the discussion naturally moves to specific terms. If it is "three years and no route back into the old industry", it has to return to direction. Either type can do this, and who proposes it first has nothing to do with type.

Worth noting: both may count money first for the family's sake, and either may suddenly change their mind at some stage. Changing one's mind is not itself evidence of type; what matters is which kind of reason gets cited when the change happens.

### INFJ and ISTJ: choosing an after-school class

(Fictional scene) A seven-year-old wants to learn drawing and also wants to learn robotics. There are only two half-days at the weekend, and a year of either is a real expense.

In this fictional scene, one approach watches the state the child is in while saying it: which idea is his own and which comes from a classmate, and where the course might lead — a childhood scheduled full, or a hobby he can inhabit on his own. The other lays out the conditions: how many minutes to get there, the price per lesson, the teacher's qualifications, whether three years is realistic, how missed lessons are made up — then takes the child to a trial lesson of each and watches whether he can sit through it. Either type can combine both kinds of evidence; which step gets taken depends on division of labour, authority and the information already in hand.

Both sides are actually collecting the same material: the child's willingness, his response in the trial, the family's time and budget, how far the course can go. The difference is which part gets picked up first and which gets trusted first. Reading only the child's eyes may sign him up for something lively that stops after two years; counting only hours and price may produce a child who dawdles at the door every week while the money is spent and nobody goes. Neither risk belongs to one type.

The review step is to ask rather than conclude on the child's behalf: after the trial, do not enrol immediately — let the child say whether he wants to come back, then ask why. A child who cannot explain is normal; book another trial or ask the teacher what they observed. Put the budget and the transport arrangement on the table at the same time, so that "wanting to" and "being able to" are visible together.

What genuinely needs agreeing in advance is when it can stop. Settling on a number of lessons before a joint review gives both an observation window and a clear exit point; the number follows the course rhythm and the household situation, and does not need to copy anyone else's figure.
sections.title: INFJ and ISTJ at work and in relationships

sections.body_md:
The first misread takes I for unsociable. An INFJ can talk until late in a one-to-one; an ISTJ tells jokes among colleagues they know. Introversion describes where attention and energy tend to go, not social performance, and not a dislike of people.

The second treats T and F as hard and soft. An ISTJ can hold a hard line about someone they care about; an INFJ can analyse cause and effect without mercy. Judging type by whether today's remarks felt warm reads the setting and the mood, not a preference. Talking about meaning and keeping to the rules are both learnable expressions, on a different layer from the four letters.

The third stops at "both have strong opinions" and calls it a shared trait. Having opinions is the surface; the source is the point. One more often works back from direction to conditions, the other forward from precedent. Without that distinction, any advice about getting along together misses.

The fourth uses who speaks or moves first as evidence. In the same household task, the person who moves first is often simply the one who knows the situation better; duty, experience and how many people are present all rewrite the order.
sections.title: INFJ and ISTJ: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When results differ between sittings, check the assessment name, item bank, language version and scoring definition first, then look at which kind of experience you were referring to while answering: projects at work, or chores at home. Circumstances push answers toward one side, and a single score cannot establish a stable tendency.

Put the practice on several comparable situations rather than one reaction. Pick three recent decisions you hesitated over and write three lines for each: which facts and precedents were trusted, which connections and possibilities were noticed, and whether the final weighing used "can this standard be applied consistently" or "what does this mean for the people involved". If one kind of evidence keeps appearing, it is worth discussing as a habit of gathering and judging — not as a rule for assigning a type.

Recording counterexamples matters just as much: on the same question you used the other kind of evidence, which shows both approaches are within reach. Keep such notes for reflection; they are not scored and do not decide a type.
sections.title: INFJ and ISTJ: how to keep observing

items.answer:
Because both sides contain the four categories — Intuition, Sensing, Thinking, Feeling — and differ only in which seat each occupies and whether it faces inward or outward.

In the four-function notation used here, INFJ is Ni–Fe–Ti–Se and ISTJ is Si–Te–Fi–Ne. Compared seat by seat, the attitudes match and the processes differ; compared by the same process, Ni against Ne for instance, the attitudes reverse and the positions move as well. The two comparisons have to be kept apart, or the conclusion becomes "all directions reversed", which fits neither the names nor the positions.
items.question: Why call these the same set of categories when no function name is shared?

items.answer:
They part on what counts as material and on the standard of judgement: one more often takes pattern and possibility as material, the other fact and precedent; one more often puts people and values into the judgement, the other applies a rule that can be used consistently.

In a fictional review, either colleague could object because a proposal puts an unfair burden on one group, or because the proposed exception fails a standard applied to everyone else. Those reasons illustrate F and T respectively. A single remark does not establish a preference.
items.question: Both are introverted and both like an arrangement — where do they part?

items.answer:
Yes. Talking about meaning and keeping to the rules are learnable expressions, on a different layer from preference, and neither can be used to assign a type.

There are ISTJs who explain to an apprentice, shortly before retiring, why the craft is worth doing; there are INFJs who file the household's receipts by year. Both types can become very good at the other side when a duty requires it. What discriminates better is ordinary life, where nobody asks and nobody reminds: which kind of information you reach for first, and which kind of standard you use to close the question.
items.question: Can an ISTJ talk about meaning, and an INFJ follow the rules?

items.answer:
One more often asks whether this path leads where they want to go; the other more often asks whether the job can be done steadily and by what rules one advances.

The blind spots on both sides are conditional: someone following direction may skip the specific wording in the terms; someone checking the terms may never ask whether they like the work. A workable move is to write one list each and swap — one headed "where I want this job to take me in three years", one headed "the fallback and the hard constraints if the worst happens". Writing both is more useful than arguing whose method is right.
items.question: In a career decision, what does each look at?

items.answer:
Not by type, but by the relative's wishes, each person's caring experience, available time and what the care actually requires — and by naming who talks, who records and who double-checks.

For example, one person talks with the relative and draws out the worries, while the other builds the rota, records medication times, and keeps the test results and reimbursement paperwork in order. That is a division of labour, not a type assignment, and the reverse arrangement is common. Keep one fixed handover in the middle, with frequency and length following changes in care rather than a fixed number. Medication, follow-up plans and whether to go to hospital are for the doctor to decide; in an emergency, seek help first, call the local emergency number and follow the dispatcher's or attending clinician's instructions, while the household's job is to bring the observed facts and records along.
items.question: How should the two divide care for an older relative?

items.answer:
First separate a type-match score from a dimension score on S/N or T/F; they are not the same thing.

If the tool does report dimension scores, the most that can be said is that this sitting showed limited separation under that tool's scoring, and the meaning is whatever the report says. If there is only a type result, with no dimension scores and no scoring notes, it cannot be inferred that there was "no preference to begin with", and still less that a change of job or relationship would flip the type. Check the item bank and the circumstances at the time, and note the situation you were referring to, so the next sitting has something to compare against.

Framework sources: preference definitions follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.themyersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type-dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

Four-position convention on this page: Ni–Fe–Ti–Se for INFJ and Si–Te–Fi–Ne for ISTJ, in particular the attitude of the third process, follow a common writing adopted here as an editorial convention. Other sources handle it differently, and this is not presented as the Foundation's only reading; where a version gives only function names without attitudes, check the source before comparing.

Editorial fiction note: the offer and the after-school class in this page are editorial fiction, used to illustrate ways of comparing preferences, and correspond to no real household, company or person.

Scope limits: this page describes emphasis between preferences. It is not a ranking of ability, and it is not for hiring screens or predicting relationships; care and medical decisions belong to qualified professionals. Assessment results are interpreted according to the notes of the tool used. The FermatMind assessment uses its own item bank and scoring, described in the [scoring and evidence note](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).
